content.title: Responses to Reviewer AzxJ
content.comment:
We appreciate your review and recognizing our paper as well-written, proposing novel mask prompt tuning, and presenting strong results. It would be much appreciated if we could get your feedback about whether we have addressed your concerns, as well as your potential rating reconsideration **before Nov 11**.
 
**Q1:** The technical novelty is limited. The only technical novelty is mask prompt tuning, whereas the overall pipeline is very similar to SimBaseline and Zegformerr.
 
**A1:** We follow and extend existing two-stage methods, such as SimBaseline and Zegformer. We first empirically show that the bottleneck of two-stage methods lies in the CLIP classification, which has not been studied before. Furthermore, unlike SimBaseline and Zegformer which directly utilize the vanilla CLIP, we propose to adapt CLIP for masked images with collected diverse mask-category pairs. Mask prompt tuning is designed for adapting to the corrupted masked images, which is another key contribution.
 
**Q2:** the idea of training on large amount of caption-available dataset is similar to that of OpenSeg.
 
**A2:** OpenSeg is one of our key reference papers as it also uses COCO caption. 
However, our method differs from OpenSeg in two major ways: (1) The network framework is different. OpenSeg only uses ALIGN’s text encoder (akin to CLIP’s text encoder) and learns region-word grounding in COCO caption from scratch. It doesn’t even use the CLIP to process masked proposals. Our method investigates the usage of CLIP and proposes to adapt it to masked proposals for segmentation. (2) We collect diverse mask-category pairs from COCO caption and propose mask prompt tuning to adapt CLIP without changing its original weights. This is also not explored by OpenSeg. Moreover, our OVSeg significantly outperforms OpenSeg with the same COCO training images. 
 
**Q3:** Moreover, OpenSeg is trained on OpenImage where masks are not available, but OVSeg is trained on COCO-Stuff where mask annotations are used.
 
**A3:** OpenSeg uses COCO pre-trained model to first generate pseudo mask labels on OpenImage and further train the model on COCO+OpenImage. Same as OpenSeg, our model can also train on OpenImage: we first generate pseudo masks and then train our model with pseudo masks, which we point to as future work. Moreover, we do not use mask annotations when we collect diverse mask-category pairs.

**Q4:** The backbone Swin-B is trained on ImageNet-21K rather than ImageNet-1K. I am not sure if it is a fair comparison to other methods, such as ZegFormer.
 
**A4:** For the top part of open-vocabulary generalist models in Tab.1, all the models use ImageNet-1K pre-trained ResNet models, including ZegFormer and our OVSeg. We train another R-50 OVSeg with COCO-Stuff-156 data for a fair comparison with ZegFormer. Our R-50 OVSeg achieves 23.2% mIoU on ADE20K-150, +6.8% higher than ZegFormer.
For the bottom part, Swin-B is initialized with ImageNet-21K pre-trained weights while OpenSeg’s EfficientNet-B7 is initialized with ALIGN checkpoint which is pre-trained with 1.8B images. Even if we add the 400M CLIP pre-training data, our OVSeg uses much fewer pre-training images than OpenSeg but achieves much higher performance.
 
 
**Q5:** When the full model is fine-tuned, the proposed mask tuning brings marginal improvement (i.e. Table 3 (c) comparing to (b)).
 
**A5:** The proposed mask prompt tuning (MPT) brings an additional +0.8% mIoU on ADE20K-150 over a fully fine-tuned model. This improvement is relatively smaller than the MPT only case (Tab.3 (a)) where we observe +4.7% mIoU on ADE20K-150. However, +0.8% mIoU on ADE20K-150 is non-trivial. For instance, replacing the supervised MaskFormer backbone from R-50 to R1-01 brings +1% mIoU improvement [1]. Since R-101 is twice larger as R-50, 0.8% mIoU is a considerable gain compared to directly scaling the model.

[1]https://github.com/facebookresearch/MaskFormer/blob/main/MODEL_ZOO.md#ade20k-semantic-segmentation

content.title: Responses to Reviewer SWXX
content.comment:
We appreciate your review and recognizing our paper as well-written, and presenting a new pretraining model. It would be much appreciated if we could get your feedback on whether we have addressed your concerns, as well as your potential rating reconsideration **before Nov 11**.
 
**Q1:** Previous methods have already used COCO-Stuff, COCO Caption, and CLIP for open-vocabulary semantic segmentation. For example, OpenSeg (Ghiasi et al., 2021) also design a two-stage model and use COCO-Stuff as well as COCO Caption for the training. 
 
**A1:** OpenSeg is one of our key reference papers as it also uses COCO caption. However, our method differs from OpenSeg in two major ways: (1) The network framework is different. OpenSeg only uses ALIGN’s text encoder (akin to CLIP’s text encoder) and learns region-word grounding in COCO caption from scratch. It doesn’t even use the CLIP to process masked proposals. Our method investigates the usage of CLIP and proposes to adapt it to masked proposals for segmentation. (2) We collect diverse mask-category pairs from COCO caption and propose mask prompt tuning to adapt CLIP without changing its original weights. This is also not explored by OpenSeg. Moreover, our OVSeg significantly outperforms OpenSeg with the same COCO training images. 

**Q2:** Therefore, the main contribution is the mask prompt tuning, but it is a modification of visual prompt tuning (Jia et al., 2022).

**A2:** Mask prompt tuning is designed for our corrupted mask images, which is another key contribution of our work. Unlike introducing additional prompts like VPT(Jia et al., 2022), our MPT replaces mask tokens with learnable prompts, thus no additional computation is needed to process one image. Moreover, we further demonstrate that prompt tuning can improve over a fully fine-tuned model. Such additional improvements have not been reported by prior work.

**Q3:** Unfair comparison. In Table 1, compared with other methods, the proposed method uses different backbones, training data and pertaining models. Can you provide a comparison with the same backbone and as the same training data as possible? That will make readers easier to understand and follow your work.
 
**A3:** We notice open-vocabulary segmentation is a new research problem, thus different approaches may use different protocols. We further add OVSeg-R101c trained with COCO-Stuff-156 in Tab.1. It has the same backbone (R101c), training data (COCO-Stuff-156), and pretraining weights (ImageNet-1k pre-trained) as SimBaseline. Our OVSeg model achieves 24.0% mIoU on ADE20K-150, outperforming SimBaseline by a large margin. Furthermore, we note the baseline model in Tab.2 and Tab.3 is very close to SimBaseline and ZegFormer. With the proposed (1) CLIP adaption with collected diverse mask-category pairs and (2) mask prompt tuning, OVSeg significantly outperforms the baseline.
 
**Q4:** Similarly, the proposed model uses different backbones and decoders when comparing with fully-supervised methods. These unfair comparisons cannot support the claim that 'generalist models can match the performance of supervised specialist models'.
 
**A4:** Sorry for the confusion. As we note in the abstract: “generalist models match the performance of supervised specialist models in 2017 without dataset specific adaptations.” Therefore, we did not claim that zero-shot OVSeg matches supervised counterparts under the same setting. Our generalist model performs zero-shot evaluation without seeing any single image in the target dataset. Thus, our generalist model performance usually is behind their fully-supervised counterparts which are directly trained on target datasets. We further update Tab.1 with the supervised MaskFormer trained on ADE20K-150 and ADE20K-847, which serves as an upper-bound reference performance. It is worth noting that zero-shot evaluation is a pretty challenging setting. The previous SOTA OpenSeg only achieves 21.1% mIoU on ADE20K-150 when trained with COCO. Our OVSeg is the first model to show that the zero-shot model is able to approach some of the early supervised models.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a novel CLIP fine-tuning method to improve its performance when used in open vocabulary semantic segmentation as a masked patch classifier. The proposed method can work in two scenarios: fully fine-tuning the CLIP model or keeping the original weight but learning a new visual prompt. 
The paper starts with an intuitive analysis of the popular two-stage paradigm for open vocabulary semantic segmentation using CLIP. Ablation analysis is conducted to justify that the performance bottleneck lies in the classification error of CLIP applied on masked image patches. The paper proposes a fine-tuning strategy for CLIP on masked images and class pairs. The paper proposes two contributions: 1. collect mask-category pairs using a semi-supervised method combing coco-stuff and coco-caption. 2. A mask visual prompt tuning strategy to fine-tune the CLIP model. The method can be used with or without changing the CLIP model itself.
 
The paper conduct extensive experiment and analysis on popular benchmarks. The proposed model can outperform some of the fully supervised model on new datasets in a zero-shot manner. Both the dataset extension and the mask prompt tuning are proven to be effective through analysis.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- The idea is intuitive and adequately backed up by analysis
- The technical section is precise and detailed.
- The paper provides a clear comparison of two closely related works: RegionCLIP; Visual Text Prompt.
- The model performance is strong.

Weakness:
- While collecting large vocabulary mask-category pairs without fine-grain annotation is interesting, coco-caption is considerably a huge dataset. It would be interesting to explore replacing coco-caption with the original CLIP model.
- [Detailed] In Table 2 method (2), it's not quite clear to me how the authors match captions (12k nouns) to ground truth mask on COCO-stuff which is defined on a 171 ontology assuming there is little error in the annotation.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper3214 by Reviewer ALTp

content.title: Responses to Reviewer ALTp
content.comment:
We appreciate your review and recognizing our paper as well-written, having intuitive ideas, and presenting strong results. We are glad to answer your questions point by point.

**Q1:** While collecting large vocabulary mask-category pairs without fine-grain annotation is interesting, coco-caption is considerably a huge dataset. It would be interesting to explore replacing coco-caption with the original CLIP model.
 
**A1:** If we understand correctly, you are suggesting using other image-caption datasets, such as original CLIP datasets instead of high-quality fine-grained COCO-caption data, to collect mask-category pairs. We did try to collect pairs from the Conceptual Captions 3M (CC-3M) dataset, which has lower-quality captions than COCO-caption. Surprisingly, with the R101c-ViTB OVSeg model,  the zero-shot performance on ADE20K-150 with CC-3M pairs is only -1.0% worse than that of COCO-caption, showing that our approach can still work well with low-quality image-caption datasets. 

**Q2:** [Detailed] In Table 2 method (2), it's not quite clear to me how the authors match captions (12k nouns) to ground truth mask on COCO-stuff which is defined on a 171 ontology assuming there is little error in the annotation.
 
**A2:** When we collect mask-category pairs, the source of mask and category nouns can be decoupled. For GT masks with 1 caption, we use GT masks to get the crop-masked regions without using GT class labels. We extract nouns from the corresponding caption and treat them as the candidate categories to pair with GT crop-masked regions. As you point out, GT masks are defined with limited 171 categories. Some visual elements in the caption may not exist in GT masks, such as the teapot in Fig.3. In this case, the teapot can only be aligned with the GT mask of apple or orange, resulting in a misleading pair. This is the reason why the proposal works better than GT masks.

content.title: Responses to Reviewer PRQy
content.comment:
We appreciate your review and recognizing our mask prompt tuning as interesting. It would be much appreciated if we could get your feedback about whether we have addressed your concerns, as well as your potential rating reconsideration **before Nov 11**.

**Q1:** At beginning, the author argues "CLIP can not perform satisfactory classification over masked images". However, later the author still "use CLIP to pair the most matching mask proposal to each class" to generate mask-category pairs.

**A1:** CLIP requires a set of candidate categories for classification. We observe that CLIP works much better if we only input the categories that exist in the image. Taking Fig.1 (b) as an example, if we only input the 5 GT categories (“bridge”, “hill”, “sand”, “sea”, “sky”) rather than all the 150 ADE categories into the CLIP text encoder, CLIP would perform much better. Specifically, the mIoU with GT categories is 42.8%, which is nearly twice the standard mIoU (21.1%). This is because using GT categories reduces the choice space of CLIP classification, turning it into a much easier problem. Returning to our mask-category pairs generation, the nouns within the captions are highly relevant to the image contents, with which CLIP can work empirically well. 
Moreover, our training process is essentially a self-training process where we bootstrap the CLIP with self-pseudo labeling. Even though our collected pairs are somehow noisy, the diverse dataset can better retain CLIP’s generalization ability. More details about noisy self-training can be found in [1].

**Q2:** It used a pre-trained maskformer to generate mask proposal. What data is used for training? Does it cover categories overlapped with evaluation datasets? How does it generate to unseen category?
 
**A2:** We use 118k COCO images with 171 class annotations to train MaskFormer. Yes, we notice there are some categories overlapping the evaluation dataset. We use the ADE20k-150 dataset as an example and analyze the mIoU of seen (overlapped) and unseen categories in Appendix A.4 and Fig.8. With the average mIoU 29.6%, the mIoU of seen and unseen categories are 37.6% and 21.9%, respectively, showing that our model can perform well on unseen categories. More importantly, our model allows users to define arbitrary queries and search for the query in the image. As shown in Fig.5, our model can locate and segment Oculus as the VR headset, and golden gate as the bridge, revealing the huge potential of open vocabulary segmentation.
 
**Q3:** Experiment in Table 1 is misleading. Since the author uses maskformer as baseline, why not directly compared with its supervised performance. How much gain is from using maskformer?
 
**A3:** Our OVSeg is not directly comparable with the supervised MaskFormer. Since a supervised MaskFormer is a closed-set specialist model, it cannot be directly evaluated on new classes or datasets. In contrast, our OVSeg is an open-vocabulary generalist model and can be evaluated on arbitrary datasets with arbitrary categories. We also update Tab.1 with the supervised MaskFormer trained on ADE20K-150 and ADE20K-847, which serves as an upper-bound reference for performance. Although our OVSeg model doesn’t see any single training image in the target dataset, it can still achieve considerably good performance.
We note that the baseline model in Tab.2 and Tab.3 is a minor modification of MaskFormer, which is close to SimBaseline and ZegFormer. With the proposed (1) CLIP adaption with collected diverse mask-category pairs and (2) mask prompt tuning, OVSeg significantly outperforms the baseline.
 
**Q4:** Experiment in Table 2 is also not clear. How does GT mask archive for 1 caption?
 
**A4:** When we collect mask-category pairs, the source of mask and category nouns can be decoupled. For GT masks with 1 caption, we use GT masks to get the crop-masked regions without using GT class labels. We extract nouns from the corresponding caption and treat them as the candidate categories to pair with GT crop-masked regions. You may notice that some visual elements in the caption may not exist in GT masks, such as the teapot in Fig.3. In this case, the teapot can only be aligned with the GT mask of apple or orange, resulting in a misleading pair. This is the reason why the proposal works better than GT masks.
 
**Q5:** Figure 2 is not illustrated. Consider remove it or provide more details.
 
**A5:** We have added a more detailed caption for Figure 2: The modified MaskFormer is trained with CLIP’s text embeddings so as to perform open-vocabulary segmentation. We use the pre-trained segmentation model to generate class-agnostic proposals and align proposals with extracted nouns from corresponding captions. After collecting diverse mask-category pairs, we fine-tune CLIP with the proposed mask prompt tuning.

[1] Xie, Qizhe, et al. "Self-training with noisy student improves imagenet classification." CVPR 2020.
